To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

interface states in hardened wet oxides are produced in a radiation dose and field-dependent manner, and that the same is true for hardened dry oxides except for the fact that the magnitude of interface-state generation in a hardened dry-oxide capacitor is considerably smaller than in a hardened wet-oxide capacitor.
the radiation-induced interface-state buildup is a function of the oxide-growth conditions and that the interface-state buildup is independent of the radiation environment.

the interface states in hardened oxides are generated during irradiation and that the interface states are generated by the same mechanisms that are responsible for interface-state generation during wet oxidation, the only difference being that the interface states generated in a dry oxide are considerably smaller than those generated in a wet oxide.
In summary, our research is concerned with
the effects of pulsed irradiation and neutron irradiation on the electrical characteristics of MOS capacitors.
the effects of radiation on the properties of silicon-oxide interfaces.
the generation of radiation-induced interface states in MOS capacitors.
In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
the buildup of interface states observed in the hardened wet oxides is due to a time-dependent annealing out of the radiation-induced oxide defects.
there is a buildup of interface states with time following pulsed irradiation, but the buildup is not significant in a neutron fluence range of ~1013 to ~1014 n/cm2.
there is no evidence that the radiation hardness of dry oxides is due to the absence of interface states.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the interface state generation in hardened oxides is a function of oxide thickness, oxide growth temperature, and the presence of a wetting layer of SiO2 at the Si-SiO2 interface.
the interface states in hardened oxides are stable at room temperature for periods of several years.
the interface states are not created by the radiation, but that the radiation merely accelerates the interface-state buildup which would have occurred anyway in the absence of radiation.
The main takeaway from our work is that
the interface-state generation mechanism is not a function of the radiation species, but rather a function of the total radiation dose and the electric field.

the interface-state buildup is not a function of the neutron fluence, but rather is a function of the radiation dose, and that the interface state buildup is a function of both the field and the radiation dose.
the buildup of interface states is a function of the radiation environment.
